title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 867–868 (Night 203, continuing nights-202), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 203 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. He pays no heed to the townspeople and keeps crying that he is the scribe, the reckoner and the astrologer; they grow angry and call him a dull, headstrong fool who should pity his youth and beauty. King al-Ghayūr hears the clamour and sends his vizier down to fetch the astrologer. Brought before the king, Qamar al-Zamān kisses the ground and recites two lines praising eight virtues. The king seats him beside him and warns him: whoever goes in to his daughter and fails to cure her loses his head, and whoever cures her marries her. Qamar al-Zamān accepts, saying he knew this before he came; the king has the judges witness it and hands him to a eunuch to take to the Lady Budūr. On the way the young man races ahead, and the eunuch, running after him, tells him he has never seen an astrologer so eager for his own ruin; Qamar al-Zamān turns his face away, and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thālithatu baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the third after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and third night,
sentences.n: The night is numbered “the third after the two hundred”: al-thālitha, “the third”, is feminine to agree with layla. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ لَمْ يَلْتَفِتْ إِلَى كَلَامِ أَهْلِ الْمَدِينَةِ وَصَارَ يُنَادِي أَنَا الْكَاتِبُ أَنَا الْحَاسِبُ أَنَا الْمُنَجِّمُ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni lam yaltafit ilā kalāmi ahli al-madīnati wa-ṣāra yunādī anā al-kātibu anā al-ḥāsibu anā al-munajjimu
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān not did-turn to (the) speech (of the) people (of) the-city, and-came-to calling-out: I (am) the-scribe, I (am) the-reckoner, I (am) the-astrologer!
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān paid no heed to what the townspeople said, but went on crying, “I am the scribe! I am the reckoner! I am the astrologer!”
sentences.n: Shahrazād picks up where the night before broke off. iltafata ilā, “to pay heed to”: ilā marks what is heeded. ṣāra yunādī, “he took to calling out”, ṣāra with the imperfect, as so often. The cry is a shortened form of the rhymed one he was taught.

sentences.t: فَاغْتَاظَ جَمِيعُ أَهْلِ الْمَدِينَةِ مِنْهُ وَقَالُوا لَهُ مَا أَنْتَ إِلَّا شَابٌّ بَلِيدٌ مُكَابِرٌ أَحْمَقُ ارْحَمْ شَبَابَكَ وَصِغَرَ سِنِّكَ وَحُسْنَكَ وَجَمَالَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-ightāẓa jamīʿu ahli al-madīnati minhu wa-qālū lahu mā anta illā shābbun balīdun mukābirun aḥmaqu irḥam shabābaka wa-ṣighara sinnika wa-ḥusnaka wa-jamālaka
sentences.l: And-became-enraged all (the) people (of) the-city at-him, and-they-said to-him: Not you (are) except a-youth dull, stubborn, foolish! Have-pity-on your-youth and-(the)-smallness (of) your-age, and-your-beauty and-your-loveliness!
sentences.i: At this all the people of the city grew angry with him and said, “You are nothing but a dull, headstrong, foolish boy! Have pity on your youth and your tender years, on your beauty and your grace!”
sentences.n: ightāẓa min, Form VIII of ghāẓa, “to be enraged at”: min marks the one who angers. mā anta illā …, “you are nothing but …”: mā … illā narrows the sentence to what follows illā; here the illā has no printed shadda. mukābir, active participle of kābara, Form III, “to defy, persist stubbornly”. aḥmaq, “foolish”, is on the afʿal pattern of adjectives of defects, and so takes no tanwīn. irḥam, “have pity on”, imperative of raḥima: the alif is the helping one, sounded i-. ṣighar al-sinn, “smallness of age”, is youth: ṣighara sinnika, “your tender years”. The four objects pair off, shabāb with sinn, ḥusn with jamāl. The shadda of سنّك is printed.

sentences.t: فَصَاحَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَقَالَ أَنَا الْمُنَجِّمُ وَالْحَاسِبُ فَهَلْ مِنْ طَالِبٍ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāḥa Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-qāla anā al-munajjimu wa-al-ḥāsibu fa-hal min ṭālibin
sentences.l: And-cried-out Qamar al-Zamān and-said: I (am) the-astrologer and-the-reckoner; so-is-there of a-seeker?
sentences.i: But Qamar al-Zamān cried out, “I am the astrologer and the reckoner! Is there anyone who seeks?”
sentences.n: hal min ṭālibin, “is there any seeker?”: after a question with hal, min before an indefinite noun means “any at all”, and the noun is genitive after it.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ يُنَادِي وَالنَّاسُ يَنْهَوْنَهُ إِذْ سَمِعَ صَوْتَهُ الْمَلِكُ الْغَيُورُ وَسَمِعَ ضَجَّةَ النَّاسِ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā Qamaru al-Zamāni yunādī wa-al-nāsu yanhawnahu idh samiʿa ṣawtahu al-maliku al-Ghayūru wa-samiʿa ḍajjata al-nāsi
sentences.l: And-while Qamar al-Zamān (was) calling-out, and-the-people forbidding-him, when heard his-voice the-king al-Ghayūr, and-heard (the) clamour (of) the-people.
sentences.i: And while Qamar al-Zamān was crying out and the people were trying to stop him, King al-Ghayūr heard his voice and the clamour of the crowd.
sentences.n: baynamā … idh, “while … then”: baynamā sets the scene, and idh brings in what happens in the middle of it. wa-al-nāsu yanhawnahu, “the people forbidding him”, a clause of state with wa-. nahā, “to forbid, try to stop”, imperfect plural yanhawna. In samiʿa ṣawtahu al-maliku the object comes before the subject; the -hu of ṣawtahu is Qamar al-Zamān. ḍajja, “clamour, uproar”; its shadda is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ لِلْوَزِيرِ انْزِلِ أ أْتِنَا بِهٰذَا الْمُنَجِّمِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku li-al-wazīri inzili iʾtinā bi-hādhā al-munajjimi
sentences.l: And-said the-king to-the-vizier: Go-down, bring-us with-this the-astrologer!
sentences.i: And the king said to the vizier, “Go down and bring me this astrologer.”
sentences.n: The print sets the second word as two pieces, أ اتنا, with a lone alif carrying a hamza and then اتنا; both are kept as printed. The likeliest reading is iʾtinā, “bring us”, the imperative of atā, ائتنا in the usual spelling: the first piece is read as the alif that opens the imperative, left without a vowel like the helping alif of inzil, since after inzili it is not sounded, and the second as the hamza of the root and the rest of the word, ʾtinā. Another reading cannot be ruled out, so the print is kept and pointed by this sense. atā bi-, “to come with”, means “to bring”: bi- marks what is brought. The two imperatives, inzil and iʾtinā, stand side by side without wa-, as in speech; inzili takes a helping kasra before the next word. The king says “us”, the plural of majesty.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَ الْوَزِيرُ سَرِيعًا وَأَخَذَ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ مِنْ وَسْطِ النَّاسِ وَأَطْلَعَهُ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-nazala al-wazīru sarīʿan wa-akhadha Qamara al-Zamāni min wasṭi al-nāsi wa-aṭlaʿahu ilā al-maliki
sentences.l: And-went-down the-vizier quickly, and-took Qamar al-Zamān from (the) midst (of) the-people, and-made-him-go-up to the-king.
sentences.i: The vizier went down at once, took Qamar al-Zamān from the midst of the crowd, and brought him up to the king.
sentences.n: sarīʿan, “quickly”, an adjective in the accusative used as an adverb. min wasṭi, “from the midst of”. aṭlaʿa, Form IV of ṭalaʿa, “to go up”, so “to make go up, bring up”; in Classical usage aṭlaʿa means rather “to show, inform”, and this sense belongs to the later language.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا صَارَ بَيْنَ يَدَىِ الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ قَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ṣāra bayna yadayi al-maliki al-Ghayūri qabbala al-arḍa wa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: And-when he-came-to-be between (the) two-hands (of) the-king al-Ghayūr, he-kissed the-ground and-recited, saying:
sentences.i: When he stood before King al-Ghayūr, he kissed the ground and recited:
sentences.n: bayna yadayi, “between the two hands of”, is “in the presence of”. yaday is the dual yadāni in construct, and it takes a linking kasra before the article; the print spells it يدى, with ى. qabbala al-arḍa, “he kissed the ground”, the courtier's homage. anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”, the usual way of bringing in verse. The shadda of قبّل is printed.

sentences.t:
ثَمَانِيَةٌ فِى الْمَجْدِ حُزْتَ جَمِيْعَهَا * فَلَا زَالَ خُدَّامًا بِهِنَّ لَكَ الدَّهْرُ
يَقِيْنُكَ وَالتَّقْوَى وَمَجْدُكَ وَالنَّدَى * وَلَفْظُكَ وَالْمَعْنِي وَعِزُّكَ وَالنَّصْرُ
sentences.tr:
thamāniyatun fī al-majdi ḥuzta jamīʿahā * fa-lā zāla khuddāman bihinna laka al-dahru
yaqīnuka wa-al-taqwā wa-majduka wa-al-nadā * wa-lafẓuka wa-al-maʿnī wa-ʿizzuka wa-al-naṣru
sentences.l:
Eight in the-glory you-have-won all-of-them; * so-may-not cease (as) servants by-them to-you the-time.
Your-certainty and-the-piety, and-your-glory and-the-generosity, * and-your-utterance and-the-meaning, and-your-might and-the-victory.
sentences.i:
Eight things there are in glory, and you have won them all: * may Time through them never cease to be your servant!
Your sure faith and your piety, your glory and your bounty, * your words and their meaning, your might and your victory.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on al-dahru / al-naṣru. The first line names a number, and the second counts the eight off in four pairs. fa-lā zāla, “so may it not cease”: lā with the perfect makes a wish; the subject is al-dahr, “Time”, held back to the end of the line, and khuddāman, “servants”, plural though dahr is singular, is the predicate of zāla. bihinna, “by them”: bi- marks the means, the eight virtues, and laka, “to you”, says whose servant. ḥāza, “to win, gain possession of”. nadā, properly “dew”, is also “generosity”. maʿnā, “meaning”, is pointed in the print as وَالْمَعْنِي, with kasra and yāʾ, al-maʿnī, where the usual form is al-maʿnā, spelt with ى; the print's pointing is kept. The print also spells fī as فِى, with ى, and sets a sukūn on the long yāʾ of جَمِيْعَهَا and يَقِيْنُكَ, as it often does.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرَ الْمَلِكُ الْغَيُورُ إِلَيْهِ أَجْلَسَهُ إِلَى جَانِبِهِ وَأَقْبَلَ عَلَيْهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ بِاللّٰهِ يَا وَلَدِي إِنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ مُنَجِّمًا فَلَا تُخَاطِرْ بِنَفْسِكَ وَلَا تَدْخُلْ عَلَى شَرْطِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẓara al-maliku al-Ghayūru ilayhi ajlasahu ilā jānibihi wa-aqbala ʿalayhi wa-qāla lahu bi-Allāhi yā waladī in lam takun munajjiman fa-lā tukhāṭir bi-nafsika wa-lā tadkhul ʿalā sharṭī
sentences.l: And-when looked the-king al-Ghayūr at-him, he-seated-him at his-side, and-turned to-him, and-said to-him: By-God, O my-son, if not you-are an-astrologer, then-do-not risk with-yourself, and-do-not enter upon my-condition.
sentences.i: When King al-Ghayūr looked at him, he seated him at his side, turned to him and said, “By God, my son, if you are no astrologer, do not stake your life, and do not take on my condition.
sentences.n: ajlasa, Form IV of jalasa, “to make sit, seat”. aqbala ʿalā, “to turn to someone”, with attention and favour. bi-Allāhi, “by God”: bi- of the oath. in lam takun, “if you are not”: lam with the jussive after in. The answer starts with fa- because it is a prohibition, fa-lā tukhāṭir. khāṭara bi-, “to risk”: the verb takes bi- for what is staked, bi-nafsika, “your life”. dakhala ʿalā sharṭī, “to enter upon my condition”, that is, to accept its terms and stake one's head. The shadda of منجّما is printed.

sentences.t: فَإِنِّي شَرَطْتُ عَلَى نَفْسِي أَنَّ كُلَّ مَنْ دَخَلَ عَلَى بِنْتِي وَلَمْ يُبْرِئْهَا مِمَّا أَصَابَهَا ضَرَبْتُ عُنُقَهُ وَكُلَّ مَنْ أَبْرَأَهَا زَوَّجْتُهُ بِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-innī sharaṭtu ʿalā nafsī anna kulla man dakhala ʿalā bintī wa-lam yubriʾhā mimmā aṣābahā ḍarabtu ʿunuqahu wa-kulla man abraʾahā zawwajtuhu bihā
sentences.l: For-indeed-I stipulated upon myself that every who entered upon my-daughter and-not cured-her from-what befell-her, I-struck his-neck; and-every who cured-her, I-married-him with-her.
sentences.i: For I have bound myself that whoever goes in to my daughter and does not cure her of what has befallen her, I will strike off his head, and whoever cures her, I will marry to her.
sentences.n: sharaṭa ʿalā nafsihi, “to lay a condition on oneself”: ʿalā marks the one bound. dakhala ʿalā, of a person, “to go in to”. kulla man …, “everyone who …”, is the noun of anna, and the sentence after it, ḍarabtu ʿunuqahu, is its predicate, with -hu pointing back to kull; the perfect has a future sense in a rule laid down. abraʾa, Form IV, “to cure”: the print shows the root's hamza in يبرئها and ابرأها. ḍaraba ʿunuqahu, “to strike his neck”, to behead. min marks what one is cured of. zawwaja bi-: the verb takes bi- for the bride, “marry him to her”; the Classical construction is zawwajtuhu iyyāhā, with two objects. The shadda of زوّجته is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَا يَغُرَّنَّكَ حُسْنُكَ وَجَمَالُكَ وَاللّٰهِ وَاللّٰهِ إِنْ لَمْ تُبْرِئْهَا لَأَضْرِبَنَّ عُنُقَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lā yaghurrannaka ḥusnuka wa-jamāluka wa-Allāhi wa-Allāhi in lam tubriʾhā la-aḍribanna ʿunuqaka
sentences.l: So-let-not deceive-you your-beauty and-your-loveliness! By-God and-by-God, if not you-cure-her, surely-I-will-strike your-neck!
sentences.i: So do not let your beauty and your grace deceive you: by God, by God, if you do not cure her, I will strike off your head!”
sentences.n: lā yaghurrannaka, “let it by no means deceive you”: lā with the jussive in its energetic form, yaghurranna, which gives the command more force. gharra, “to deceive, delude”. wa-Allāhi, “by God”: wa- of the oath, with the genitive, said twice for weight. in lam tubriʾhā, “if you do not cure her”, the ئ printed. Because the oath comes first, the answer goes to the oath: la-aḍribanna, “I will surely strike”, la- of the oath and the energetic ending -anna. The shaddas of يغرّنك and لاضربنّ are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ لَكَ ذٰلِكَ وَأَنَا رَاضٍ وَعِنْدِي عِلْمُ هٰذَا قَبْلَ أَنْ آتِيَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Qamaru al-Zamāni laka dhālika wa-anā rāḍin wa-ʿindī ʿilmu hādhā qabla an ātiyaka
sentences.l: And-said Qamar al-Zamān: For-you (is) that, and-I (am) content; and-with-me (was the) knowledge (of) this before that I-come-to-you.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said, “You shall have that, and I am content: I knew of this before ever I came to you.”
sentences.n: laka dhālika, “that is yours”, that is, “agreed”. rāḍin, “content”, active participle of raḍiya; the final yāʾ falls before the tanwīn. ʿindī ʿilmu hādhā, “with me is the knowledge of this”, the usual way to say “I know this”: ʿinda marks what one has. qabla an ātiyaka, “before I came to you”: an with the subjunctive, which here looks back. The madda of آتيك and the ḍamma of علمُ are printed.

sentences.t: فَأَشْهَدَ عَلَيْهِ الْمَلِكُ الْغَيُورُ الْقُضَاةَ وَسَلَّمَهُ إِلَى الْخَادِمِ وَقَالَ لَهُ أَوْصِلْ هٰذَا إِلَى السِّتِّ بُدُورَ
sentences.tr: fa-ashhada ʿalayhi al-maliku al-Ghayūru al-quḍāta wa-sallamahu ilā al-khādimi wa-qāla lahu awṣil hādhā ilā al-sitti Budūra
sentences.l: And-made-witness against-him the-king al-Ghayūr the-judges, and-handed-him to the-eunuch, and-said to-him: Convey this to the-lady Budūr.
sentences.i: Then King al-Ghayūr called the judges to witness against him, handed him over to the eunuch and said, “Take this man to the Lady Budūr.”
sentences.n: ashhada, Form IV of shahida, “to make someone a witness”: the judges are its object, and ʿalayhi, “against him”, marks the one the witness will bind. sallama ilā, “to hand over to”. awṣala, Form IV of waṣala, “to make arrive, take”. al-sitt, “the lady”, is the later word for sayyida, used of the princess. Budūr is diptote, -a in the genitive. The shadda of سلّمه is printed.

sentences.t: فَمَسَكَهُ الْخَادِمُ مِنْ يَدِهِ وَمَشَى بِهِ فِي الدِّهْلِيزِ فَسَابَقَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-masakahu al-khādimu min yadihi wa-mashā bihi fī al-dihlīzi fa-sābaqahu Qamaru al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And-took-hold-of-him the-eunuch by his-hand and-walked with-him in the-passage; and-raced-him Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: The eunuch took him by the hand and led him along the passage, but Qamar al-Zamān hurried on ahead of him.
sentences.n: masaka, “to take hold of”, is the spoken form of Classical amsaka, Form IV; min yadihi, “by his hand”, with min marking the part taken hold of. mashā bihi, “walked with him”: bi- marks the one led along. dihlīz, a Persian word, “passage, vestibule”. sābaqa, Form III of sabaqa, “to race, try to get ahead of”.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ الْخَادِمُ يَجْرِي وَيَقُولُ لَهُ وَيْلَكَ لَا تَسْتَعْجِلْ عَلَى هَلَاكِ نَفْسِكَ فَإِنِّي مَا رَأَيْتُ مُنَجِّمًا يَسْتَعْجِلُ عَلَى هَلَاكِ نَفْسِهِ غَيْرَكَ وَلٰكِنَّكَ لَمْ تَعْرِفْ أَيُّ شَيٌ قُدَّامَكَ مِنَ الدَّوَاهِي
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra al-khādimu yajrī wa-yaqūlu lahu waylaka lā tastaʿjil ʿalā halāki nafsika fa-innī mā raʾaytu munajjiman yastaʿjilu ʿalā halāki nafsihi ghayraka wa-lākinnaka lam taʿrif ayyu shayun quddāmaka mina al-dawāhī
sentences.l: And-came the-eunuch running and-saying to-him: Woe-to-you! Do-not hasten toward (the) destruction (of) yourself; for-indeed-I not saw an-astrologer hastening toward (the) destruction (of) himself other-than-you. But-you not knew what thing (is) before-you of the-calamities.
sentences.i: The eunuch fell to running after him, saying, “Woe to you, do not hurry to your own ruin! I never saw an astrologer hurry to his own ruin but you. But you do not know what calamities lie ahead of you.”
sentences.n: ṣāra yajrī wa-yaqūlu, “he took to running and saying”, ṣāra with the imperfect. waylaka, “woe to you!”, here more alarm than curse. istaʿjala, Form X, “to hurry”; with ʿalā, “to hurry toward”, a later usage where Classical says istaʿjala alone or with bi-. halāk, “ruin, perishing”. mā raʾaytu … ghayraka, “I have not seen … other than you”, that is, “you are the only one I have seen”: ghayr is put last, the way speech does. lam taʿrif, “you do not know”, lam with a present sense here. ayyu shayun quddāmaka, “what thing is before you”, an indirect question; Classical grammar wants shayʾin, genitive after ayy, but the print sets tanwīn ḍamma on شيٌ, which is kept; the spelling شي without hamza is the edition's usual one. ayy shī, “what”, is also the spoken word for “what”. quddāma, “in front of”, a later word for amāma; mina al-dawāhī, “of calamities”, says what the “thing” is. The shaddas of ولكنّك, ايّ and قدّامك and the hamza of رأيت are printed.

sentences.t: فَأَعْرَضَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ بِوَجْهِهِ عَنِ الْخَادِمِ
sentences.tr: fa-aʿraḍa Qamaru al-Zamāni bi-wajhihi ʿani al-khādimi
sentences.l: And-turned-away Qamar al-Zamān with-his-face from the-eunuch.
sentences.i: But Qamar al-Zamān turned his face away from the eunuch.
sentences.n: aʿraḍa ʿan, Form IV, “to turn away from”; bi-wajhihi, “with his face”: bi- marks the part turned.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
